newsitem.title: USA: Columbia mission extended, jammed hatch a setback.
newsitem.headline: Columbia mission extended, jammed hatch a setback.

text.p: NASA on Monday extended the mission of the space shuttle Columbia by a day, hoping to build on the success of a star-gazing telescope that is tailing the shuttle through space.

Columbia's flight, marred by a faulty hatch that forced the cancellation of two spacewalks, was extended to Friday to allow the orbiting Orfeus-Spas telescope to gather more information. The shuttle had been due back on Earth Thursday but was rescheduled to land at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 8:02 a.m. EST (1302 GMT) Friday.
In a late-night news conference from the shuttle deck, mission commander Ken Cockrell said the five-member crew was "very, very happy" with the mission, despite the jammed hatch.
"This flight has shown us that every once in a while life throws you a little bit of a curve," he said. "We would like to think it's not the curve that counts but how we react to it."

The Orfeus-Spas, a joint U.S.-German project released from Columbia on Nov. 19, trails the spacecraft by about 26 mile (41 km). The telescope, which is studying interstellar matter to learn more about the life cycles of stars, will be left in orbit for nearly a day longer than planned before being gathered in by the shuttle at 3:26 a.m. EST (0826 GMT) Wednesday.

The extension of the planned 16-day science mission followed a weekend of frustration. On Saturday NASA managers cancelled two scheduled spacewalks after it became apparent engineers could not immediately solve the problem of a stuck airlock hatch -- the first time in the 15-year history of the shuttle programme that astronauts encountered problems with the hatch.

Astronauts Tammy Jernigan and Tom Jones, who were set to make the spacewalks, expressed frustration and disappointment at the cancellation and said it was a setback for space station construction planning.

Jernigan and Jones had expected to make two space walks to practice construction of the planned international space station due to start next November. They had planned to test tools and an 18-foot (5.5-metre) crane needed to install large components of the NASA-led, 13-nation space station.
Jones said NASA had a "very tough course ahead" to build the space station and the hatch problem was an example of the kind of issue astronauts would have to deal with successfully.
"We can't afford to bring up a major element of the station and not be able to deploy it because of being stymied by a mechanical malfunction like this," he said. "We have to find ways around them."

The two, who trained for the mission for 10 months, spent two hours in the airlock on Thursday trying to free the hatch. Yet despite the trouble, Jernigan said she would accept another spacewalking assignment.
"If the opportunity arose to go and test this hardware on another flight in the near future ... Tom and I would be happy to do that," she said. "In a heartbeat," Jones added.

NASA investigators initially suspected the problem could be that the latching mechanism, which is located outside the cabin, had become misaligned with its frame. But Jernigan said on Monday the gearing on the inside hub of the hatch was also a potential problem and expressed confidence NASA engineers would get to the bottom of it once Columbia returned to Earth.

Jernigan, Jones and astronaut Story Musgrave spent time early on Monday in the shuttle's middeck area, successfully using a tool that would have been tested in the spacewalks. The battery-operated "power grip" was used to remove bolts in a simulation of space station assembly techniques.
